name: Hot hand fallacy
statement: The belief that a basketball player who has just made several shots is more likely to make the next one was declared a cognitive illusion in 1985.
meaning: Two separate claims travel under one name, and keeping them apart is the whole story. The first is about players: that a run of hits raises the chance of the next hit. The second is about observers: that the run tells them nothing, so believing in it is an error of reasoning. Gilovich, Vallone and Tversky argued the first was false and the second therefore true. The name of the entry belongs to the second claim. It survives only for as long as the first one fails.

origin.who: Thomas Gilovich, Robert Vallone and Amos Tversky
origin.note: Their paper is "The hot hand in basketball: On the misperception of random sequences". They found no dependence between successive shots and concluded that the widespread belief in streak shooting was, in words Miller and Sanjurjo quote from page 313, "a powerful and widely shared cognitive illusion".

evidence: Three datasets and a survey, described by Tversky and Gilovich in Chance in 1989. For nine Philadelphia 76ers across 48 home games of the 1980-81 season, the chance of a hit was .51 after a hit and .54 after a miss, with eight of the nine players shooting better after a miss. Free throws for nine Boston Celtics over two seasons showed no dependence between the first shot and the second. In the controlled experiment, 14 men and 12 women from Cornell each took 100 shots from a distance where they made about half, giving .47 after a hit and .48 after a miss, with a mean serial correlation of .02. Against that, 100 avid fans from Cornell and Stanford were near unanimous: 91% said a player has a better chance after making his last two or three shots, and for a hypothetical 50% shooter they put the figure at 61% after a make and 42% after a miss. Fans also read streaks into randomness, classifying a perfectly random sequence as streak shooting 65% of the time.

replication.headline: The statistic the 1985 paper rested on is biased downwards, and correcting it turns the finding round.
replication.detail: Miller and Sanjurjo proved in Econometrica in 2018 that the proportion of successes on the trials following a streak of successes is a biased estimator of the underlying probability, even for a fair coin. Selecting the trials that follow a streak is a selection rule, and it favours sequences in which those trials are failures. The bias grows with streak length and shrinks with sequence length, and it is large at the sizes the literature uses. For a shooter taking 100 shots with a fixed 50% chance, the expected gap between shooting after three hits and after three misses is not zero but minus 8 percentage points. Gilovich and colleagues' Cornell players averaged .49 after three hits and .45 after three misses, a paired t-test on which Miller and Sanjurjo reproduce at p = .49. Correcting each player's difference for the bias implied by his or her own shooting percentage and shot count moves the average from +3 to +13 percentage points, with a standard error of 4.7 points and p < .01. Nineteen of 25 players then point the right way, and five reach individual significance. Longer streaks give +10 points at four hits and shorter ones +5.4 points at two.

study.cite: Miller, J. B., & Sanjurjo, A. (2018). Surprised by the hot hand fallacy? A truth in the law of small numbers. Econometrica, 86(6), 2019-2047.

limits: The correction is arithmetic and nobody disputes it. How much hot hand the corrected data show is another matter. Ritzwoller and Romano rebuilt the analysis on permutation tests, which carry no bias by construction, and rejected random shooting in the Cornell data at streak lengths of two and three, p = .040 and p = .004 on the difference statistic. Drop one outlier, a shooter who missed nine in a row and later made 16 in a row, and only one of those tests still clears 5%. Their power calculations say every existing controlled experiment is too small to measure the effect rather than merely detect it. Game data has not settled either. Lantis and Nesson, over 12 NBA seasons, found a small hot hand in free throws and none in field goals, where longer streaks of makes lowered the chance of the next one. Pelechrinis and Winston, using optical tracking of about 200,000 shots a season and 153 players with at least 1,000 shots, found 24 players with a hot hand after one make and 41 after four, while the league-wide adjusted effect ran the other way at minus 1.4 to minus 2.7 percentage points. Miller and Sanjurjo also report that a close replication of the Cornell study by Avugos and colleagues reverses on correction, but they could not obtain the raw data and worked from the published table.
misreadings: The overturning is about the evidence, not about basketball. What collapsed is the 1985 inference, because the test used to reach it cannot come out at zero under its own null hypothesis. That is a property of the estimator, not a coding error or a selective report, and it went unnoticed for three decades by people checking the arithmetic. Reading the reversal as proof that players get hot goes further than the data. In-game field goal records still show no positive dependence, and the strongest evidence sits in controlled shooting, where the sample sizes are small enough that a single streaky player moves the result. The second misreading is the mirror of the first. Showing that the belief is not baseless does not show it is calibrated. Fans in 1985 put a 50% shooter at 61% after a make and 42% after a miss, which is a stronger effect than the corrected shooting data show, on a question the survey and the experiment did not pose the same way. Whether people overrate the effect they are detecting is the question the field is left with, and Ritzwoller and Romano report finding no study that measures beliefs and shooting on a scale that allows the comparison.
